utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I've asked for the witness to be kept out of court for just a couple of minutes this morning, and I'm here today with the Prosecutor. We seek a little assistance, not of course any question of rearguing a topic, but we seek a little assistance in relation to the decision given on the 10th of April about the time available to the Prosecution to present its case. The decision may be found on the LiveNote transcript at 2779, and I think the official transcript starts at 2782. The concern of the Prosecutor arises, of course, from our duty to present this case, which is indeed set out in the decision that the Chamber gave, and we understand informally that there may be no written decision and it will be this decision to which we must work. So that of course we understand as we do that the Chamber is still considering ways in which evidence can properly be put forward, but the Prosecutor's concerned in light of what is said about the difficulties that face an accused who defends himself which wouldn't face others, bearing in mind that it remains her duty to prove the case. And it's with those matters in mind that we are particularly concerned about the meaning of the word "should," where Your Honour said "We decided that the Prosecution should have one year from today to conclude their case." The Chamber will understand that we -- we need to know exactly where we are. I have to say that we are doing as we have been from the start of this case everything that's in our power to conduct it in a compact way and to bring the Prosecution's case to as early a conclusion as may be, and that of course underlay the motion that I put in before this decision was announced. But it's the word "should" that we would be grateful for some assistance with, if possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If it's not clear, let me make it plain. That is a mandatory order. It is, of course, subject to the unexpected. If there are matters such as matters of illness or other unforeseen circumstance, it may have to be reviewed in the light of that circumstance, but the intention is that that is an order and not any sort of invitation or exhortation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I'm just checking if there is any other (indiscernible).

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you very much. The witness can come back subject only to this -- there has been an additional piece of paper that came to our attention over the weekend in our continuing search for material that may be Rule 68 in accordance with the system that has been in operation by the Registry that has already been handed, I think, to the accused. But since he doesn't have lawyers representing him and since he's possibly got a lot of papers before him, I want to be quite sure that he knows he's got it. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Let me deal with two other administrative matters dealing with that timing. Friday, the hearings will be 9.00 until 12.45. Next Monday, one of our members has a medical appointment in the afternoon, and we will arrange sittings between 9.00 and 3.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will have the witness, please. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to comment. It's absurd that for 14 months -- that 14 months is set as being an insufficient framework for the presentation of this so-called indictment. Second, this only proves its true character. Second, regardless of the fact that you discussed last week some alleged possibilities for me of communicating with my associates and data gathering, up until the present day, I have not been able to, either in the course of this weekend, to present my associates with any kind of information or to establish contact with a view to preparing material by them, and the explanation I was given why I was not able to do that is that you did not make a ruling or decision to that effect and that therefore, I am not in a possibility -- in -- I'm not able to inform them of any facts or about any of the material that I have received. So I don't understand how they say that no decision or ruling exists on the matter if you discussed it in court last week. And I also have another comment to make, an objection. I'm still being sent all the documents in English, and as you know, it is your duty to provide me with the documents in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let me deal with those matters. The first is the time limits for the Prosecution. That's not a matter for you at all. It's a matter for the Court to determine. Second, the explanation you were given as to why you should not communicate with your associates was the correct one. A decision has not yet been made. It will be, and you will be told of it. Third, we'll look at the position about documents being disclosed to you. Mr. Nice, perhaps you could just briefly help us with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I don't know which particular category of documents he's referring to when he says they're only being disclosed to him in English. If he's more specific I will be able to deal with it. We are as a concession and only to help him because he refuses to look at documents, I think still serving him with witness statements of upcoming witnesses shortly before they come to give evidence, and we continue to honour our 68 disclosure in the conscientious way we've done this morning. Those go to him by and large in the languages of the Tribunal. And incidentally, I think that the time may come when the Chamber will want to review an earlier decision it made about languages that the accused understands. And although I realise that the earlier decision was made, a decision that the material had to be provided to him in Serbian or B/C/S, because it wasn't then known necessarily how competent he was in the English language. It's now perfectly clear on many occasions that he is indeed fluent in the English language. He worked for a long time in America, and of course he may prefer to speak in his own language, one understands that, but given the enormous amount of expenditure there is on translation, given the enormous amount of money that we are spending time and resources that are being expended in providing him with material twice as often as the Rules require because he declines to look at the material, the Chamber may think that the time has come to review any decision that is premised on the suggestion that he doesn't understand English when he clearly does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, let us look at that in due course. The witness is here and we should continue with his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic. Cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We once again heard an untruth. I did not work in America. That is incorrect. And secondly, even if I do understand what it says in the documents, it does not mean that my associates, who are there to gather information and data for me need necessarily understand it -- them. And I can't be used as a translator and interpreter for them. And I don't see why it is not their duty to translate the documents in Serbian. There is a friend of the Court here who also requires the documents in the Serbian language. So I think this is completely out of order to enter into polemics as to whether I should be given witness statements in English or any other language. Thank you. Now, I have understood that we can continue -- I may continue with the cross-examination. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to continue where we left off, and that is the following: We can see that through the questions that I asked on the basis of the statements, on the one hand the members of the Verification Mission, and you were the executive head of that mission as we noted, and on the other hand, on the basis of statements made by different terrorist chiefs from Kosovo and Metohija to the effect that the mission served a purpose and that was to save the terrorist activity in Kosovo and Metohija, to regard the army, as Melo Dinaj [phoen] said in the quotation I made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the question? You're putting, are you, that the -- wait a moment. Wait a moment. On the basis of statements made by terrorist chiefs, the mission served a purpose and that was to save the terrorist activity. Is that what you're putting, Mr. Milosevic, as the purpose of the mission?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. I am saying that the purpose and aim of the mission was without a doubt the preparation of pre-conditions, a pretext for a war against Yugoslavia. That is my first point. And my second point is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Don't -- you're here to ask questions, not to make points. Now, there are two points you seem to be making or two questions you're asking, which should be put to the witness, and I will put them. Wait a moment -- just wait a moment, Mr. Milosevic. It's not fair for the witness that you put these things to him. He should have a chance to answer. One is -- General, will you help us with this: One, it is suggested that the purpose was, as you've heard, in relation to terrorist activity, to save it. And the second is that it was to prepare the ground or as a pretext for a war against Yugoslavia. I don't know if you can deal with those matters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The purpose of the mission was to go in and to verify the -- the agreement that had been made between the OSCE and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, which -- and that the agreement was one of the earlier documents that I alluded, I referred to. We felt that we were there to ensure that no war took place. If you recall, in the course of September and early October of 1998, things were indeed tense in the region, and there was a great deal of activity which was looking extremely ominous. NATO did issue certain orders which were made public and which indicated preparation. In the course of that, the agreement between the OSCE and the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was made in order to defuse the tension and to attempt a return to normality or a more normal situation. That was certainly how we saw our role, and we expended a considerable amount of effort in attempting to deal evenhandedly with all of the people we came in contact with. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of a statement made - and that's where we left off - by Haradinaj because I want to prove the thesis that Mr. May brought up a moment ago, that is to say, he interpreted it, that they -- in order to act against Serbia, it was necessary, in order to convince the broad international community to take action against Serbia, it was necessary to usurp or to close off Kijevo and Decani, Prilep, and so on. So Kijevo, Decani, Prilep, those are the places mentioned here. They're all well known places where they caused enormous brutalities and conflicts, atrocities, and those places are known precisely for the fact that the army of Yugoslavia and the Yugoslav security forces was accused precisely for the events that took place in those places. Now, is it true that their role was to cause as much bloodshed and conflict as possible and that this should then be verified as being the responsibility of the Yugoslav security forces? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I reminded you of his statement that the arrival of the verificators in Kosovo enabled the revival of the KLA, and he even said that the agreement saved the KLA. And then he also said that it did a lot of it to revive the army. He says revive the army. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an opinion which is not mine, and I have not heard of that statement before today, or before Friday when it was first mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This was published in his book and in interviews and so on and so forth, just like many others who, after the occupation of Kosovo, considered that they were in a position to say everything and anything that was to their advantage.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, is it incorrect?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment, that is not a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was not a question. We can no longer afford the time for statements from this accused and he is simply again using time to make statements. We must object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well that's -- very well, Mr. Nice. The objection is noted. Mr. Milosevic, you hear the point which the Prosecution take. They're right to take it. You can make your speeches in due course, not now. The witness is here, and he should be asked questions.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These are exclusively questions, and they are the subject we're discussing regardless of the fact that neither you nor the Prosecution like to hear this. And when we're talking about wasting time, we heard the other side --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is not -- that is not a proper comment. Now, it would be simpler if you just asked questions. One way one could tell if it's a question is if it's short, which it should be. We'll all get on more quickly.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I hope the answer's too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Perhaps, General, you would bear that in mind too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, going on from your last answer, I make mention of his statement, namely the talks that were held with military observers, as he says, of different armies, and especially the English, American, French, and Canadian armies. Now, were those negotiations and talks with a view to an explanation and along the lines of the explanation I made or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were regular meetings between people who had been assigned to liaise with the insurgents, with the Kosovo Liberation Army, because we needed to have regular lines of communication with them so that when incidents occurred we could rapidly get in touch with -- with them as with everyone else in an incident in order to find out precisely what had happened and to defuse the incident as quickly as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how then can we explain what he says at this end and in explaining the meetings? And he says, "The pre-preparations of NATO for an air campaign was to follow" was a separate subject discussed and that that was the contents of the talks. How can we explain that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that the liaison officers assigned by me went to the Kosovo Liberation Army to discuss NATO's preparations for an air campaign. I simply don't believe it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you believe that when speaking of forms of cooperation between the KLA and NATO during the bombing he says, during this period, in the military sense, Kosovo was a joint field for NATO and the KLA. I had advantage, I reaped advantage from the airstrikes and NATO reaped advantage through our activities against the Serb forces, and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the first month of the air campaign, I was in Macedonia, not in Kosovo. I left Macedonia on the 24th of April and did not return for the rest of the air campaign. So I was not in Kosovo during the air campaign.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And did you know, when you communicated with people of that kind such as Haradinaj, Thaci and others, do you know that they were accused, and I have here a decision for 75 -- for example, that same Haradinaj and the killings, 75 killings, group killings, individual killings, the looting of Serbs, Albanians, policeman and so on. Did you know at the time the kind of people that you were communicating with, and cooperating with. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were well aware that they were an insurgent organisation, and we were well aware that they were killing policemen, and at no stage during our time in Kosovo did we ever condone the killing of policemen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you consider them to be a terrorist organisation or an insurgent organisation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think insurgent is a better word because it's less emotive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you consider that terrorist is an emotional and emotive word, do you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that hold true for all terrorists throughout the world or just for the Kosovo terrorists?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The only ones I've met face-to-face were the ones in Kosovo. So that's the basis of my judgement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in that connection, let us go back for a moment to what you've just been saying as to the goals of the mission. Do you happen to know the Sunday Times articles on the 12th of March, 2000, in which it says that the European diplomats who worked at the time for the OSCE claim that the organisation has been played out by American policy which rendered airstrikes an unavoidable act?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We felt we were there to ensure that the situation did not get worse so that things like airstrikes did not have to happen. But we were certainly not feeling that we were being played out by American policy, as you -- as you state, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And the French paper L'Humanite wrote about it on the 18th of November, 1999, and in their articles the following was stated: That the vice-president of the parliamentary assembly of the OSCE, a German, his name was Billibina [phoen], he accused the USA that with the help of Great Britain they were undermining the OSCE mission, and here I have a quotation: "Everybody in the OSCE knew that NATO and the USA and Britain did not wish the mission to be a success. I have heard much testimony of people saying that the American instructors trained the Albanian fighters. They explained to them that it was strategically wise to killing Serb policemen in order to cause repression of large dimensions over the Albanian community." That was -- those were the words of the verifier. "I met two colleagues in the field who were doing their tasks -- who were engaged in their tasks of photographing a radar. I thought that our mission had ended when some people thought that they had collected enough data for the start of the bombing." Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it really isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is the following true, what he says, that everybody in the OSCE knew that NATO and that the USA and Britain in the first place did not want our mission to succeed. Those words, is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, absolutely not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was there discussion in the mission along these lines? If you can throw some light on this. These reports apparently were given to journalists and appear to have come from people on the mission, although that may or may not be so. Were views along these lines expressed at the time?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The OSCE is a very broad church, sir, and we were there with the people that were given to us by the sending states, and everybody had their opinion, yes. And it was not an area in which free speech was rigorously stamped down upon. And so within the mission, there were a variety of views of what the -- the potential of the mission to keep going and to do its job was. Some people were more optimistic than others. Some were more determined than others to make it work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Sunday Times in March 2000 says as follows: "The American intelligence agents recognise the fact that they have helped in the preparation and training of the KLA before NATO bombed Yugoslavia. This recognition caused bitterness on the part of European diplomats who said that this undermined efforts for a political solution to the conflict between the Serbs and the Albanians." Do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never came across these American agents who were training the Kosovo Liberation Army. I heard the odd rumour of individual misguided people who were with the Kosovo Liberation Army who were not from that region. They were not described to me as American, and I never met them, but there were persistent rumours that there were one or two people in a soldier of fortune role with the Kosovo Liberation Army. As I say, I never saw them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider that CIA agents did not take part in your mission?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: None were identified as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to the writings of the British press, your press, Walker acknowledged that the CIA almost certainly took part in the days before the airstrike. Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you need to talk to Walker about this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Is Mr. Walker a witness? You must remind me.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It's not a matter that I'm in a position to deal with at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that the functionaries of the CIA supervised the truce in Kosovo in 1998 and 1999 and had links with the KLA and gave out American manuals for fighting the Serb army and the Serb police? And this is something that appeared in the Sunday Times. The Sunday Times wrote about it. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I'm not aware of it. And I do have to say, I don't believe absolutely everything that I read in the Sunday Times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is what it says afterwards true, in continuation, when the OSCE withdrew from Kosovo one week before the airstrikes last year, many of its satellite telephones and systems for global location were given secretly to the KLA for use, which -- for the commanders -- enabled the commanders of the guerrillas to remain in contact with NATO and KLA in Washington and KLA had mobile telephones and the mobile telephone of General Clark, too. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The KLA certainly had access to satellite phones, yes. We did not leave phones behind for them. They already had them. And when we moved -- when we evacuated the mission down to Macedonia, we received information via those phones which we had not left with them but which they had anyway of what was going on in terms of human rights abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did you get that information from, from the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: In some circumstances, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Sunday Times also states that the KLA recognised that it had long-term links with American and British intelligence services. Shaban Shamata, who is included in the attempt to destabilise villages where the majority Albanian population in Serbia stated that in 1996, in Northern Albania, he had a meeting with the British, American, and Swiss with -- with American, British, and Swiss agents. Is that incorrect as well? So the essence of it is -- what I'm asking you is links with American and European intelligence services. Would you say that that was incorrect as well?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was in Germany and Sarajevo in 1996. I was not in Northern Albania. I simply don't know anything about this, and indeed I didn't even know that the Swiss had secret agents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Agim Ceku, the commander of the KLA, established contacts with the Americans in the course of his work in the Croatian army, which was modernised with the help of this cooperation for professional resources and the -- it is MPRI, a company specialised in military training and equipment, and the staff of that company spent some time in Kosovo together with other companies, Dincor [phoen] was another company, which helped in the programme for training and equipping the Bosnian army. Are you aware of the journeys of members of that company to Kosovo, both those two companies and their staff to Kosovo? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware of both companies. Dincor was the contractor through whom the Americans hired the people that they contributed to the Kosovo Verification Mission, because they had an internal difficulty in not being able to second serving military to the Kosovo Verification Mission. So they were taken on individually by Dincor and then further seconded to the OSCE. The MPRI organisation, as far as I'm aware, was in Bosnia runnings the train and equip programme. That was running down and shedding quite a lot of manpower, and some of the people who worked for MPRI stopped working for MPRI in Bosnia and applied to Dincor to become members of the Kosovo Verification Mission in a different capacity and some of them were taken on. To a degree, I believe it was a matter of expediency that these were American people who had some knowledge of the region, in some cases spoke the language, and were available very quickly. And so Dincor took them on and they worked for Dincor when they were with us. I'm not aware that MPRI had a presence in Kosovo at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that both of these companies that worked in Bosnia were transferred to work in Kosovo, to be involved in the same kind of work in Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Kosovo. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not what I'm saying. I'm saying that the MPRI hired people in Bosnia to do a job. That job finished in the course of 1998. Some of these people were taken on by Dincor to do a different job within the Kosovo Verification Mission. For MPRI in Bosnia, they were teaching the federation army tactics. In Kosovo working with Dincor, they were verifiers with our mission the same as the rest of us were. There was emphatically no training carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You are categorical in that, are you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. To the best of my knowledge, that is how I remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 18th of November, 1999, the French newspaper L'Humanite says that the vice-president of the parliamentary Assembly of the OSCE, Willy Wimmer, accused the USA for undermining the mission in Kosovo in conjunction with Great Britain. There is a quotation from there: "In every possible way they sabotaged the peace plan that the OSCE had worked on patiently. They supported the members of the KLA who were fighting instead of supporting Rugova's moderates. The Yugoslav side supported the peace plan from October, but the KLA systematically violated it, and this obviously did not suit the purposes of some circles." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not to the best of my knowledge. When the agreement was signed in October 1998, it was very much the intention that there should be a similar agreement between the OSCE and the Kosovo Albanian community, and strenuous efforts were made by Ambassador Chris Hill, an American diplomat, to get such agreement. That effort went on well into December of 1998 before it was finally concluded that it was not going to be possible to get such an agreement. We were very keen that such an agreement should happen, and a lot of contact was made with Rugova to attempt to get him to take a more leading role in -- in Kosovo at the time, which he was rather reluctant to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The same newspaper writes about the testimony of a verifier who said, "I have heard many testimonies of many people who claim that American instructors were training Albanian fighters. They explained to them that it is strategically wise to kill Serb policemen in order to cause large-scale repression over the Albanian community." Are you aware of that or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were entirely opposed to the idea of the KLA killing policemen. We made it clear to them that this was not the way to gain any support for their cause and that to kill the policemen of a sovereign state inside that state is emphatically wrong, and we said so many, many times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: They also assert that the KLA forced the Kosovars to join refugee convoys in order to make the west react as soon as possible in this way. The local security of the OSCE compiled reports on local observers and later on these reports were destroyed. They carefully recorded the attitude of each and every individual towards the KLA. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of surveys done by different pieces of the mission. I'm not aware of all of them. No, I'm not aware of every one of them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the following, Deutsche Welle, Dr. Albishtar [phoen] for the strategic studies centre from the university in Zurich, on the 5th of December, 2000, he spoke about the role of intelligence services, the CIA, at a very early stage built its connections. This is well known from the talks that were held last year in Switzerland. The KLA was practically trained by an American organisation during the war and inter alia it consisted of former officers of professional army. This link exists and links to other intelligence services are something that I am not aware of. This is what Dr. Albert Stahl claims from the centre of strategic studies from the university in Zurich. On the 5th of December, 2000 for the Deutsche Welle... Not -- are you aware of this? Not Stahl's claims, but again I'm asking you about the substance of this, his claim, rather, what he is saying, is it correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of CIA activity training the KLA, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Although the German newspaper says that CIA agents who before the attack on Yugoslavia supported and helped the KLA --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, there's no point. The point has been made. The witness has said he is not aware of it. So we need to move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this is the core of the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be, but as far as this witness is concerned, he's said he's not aware of it. He can't help us any more. If you've got evidence about it you can call it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Have you heard of Heinz Lockweih, a retired Brigadier General of the Bonn Vizier, who until 2000 was a member of the German delegation to the OSCE in Vienna? He also participated in the negotiations on arms control on the basis of Dayton, and he also published a book, and he -- "Hans Hien Lacra" [phoen], he published another book, "A War That Could Have Been Avoided". Have you heard of him?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but there's an awful lot of retired brigadiers from the German army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: He published a book. That's why I had assumed that you -- well, he claims that the KLA enjoyed unequivocal support of the West?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I raise a point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And it's a point that rises in stark form with this question that's about to start, but it arises with all the material that's been put in this morning. The accused is clearly cross-examining on extracts of material rather than putting in the material in full. That's always a problem. It's true it saves a lot of time, but the proper way to put material in is to put in the whole document so that one can check on its context, and we've had earlier examples of the accused cross-examining significantly out of context in relation to documents. But when we come to an example like this and he asks of a particular work, whether the witness knows the author, if the witness doesn't know the author, what conceivable value can there be at this stage in going on and trying to ask him about the contents of a book which the witness hasn't reviewed, we won't be able to review to check on its context, and takes us no further?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It depends on what the book says. It may be that the witness can answer the question, maybe not, but we don't know what the question is. It's not -- it's not -- in cross-examination, of course, it's not the question that matters, it's the answer. Now, it may be that the witness can assist on a particular point. He may or may not. But one has to bear in mind in this case that this is an accused in person, a litigant in person, and therefore the rules which are applied to a professional advocate have to be considered in that light. He must be entitled to some leeway. But of course sources should be identified so that you can check them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Preferably presented at the time so we can look at them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: True. Yes. What is it you want to put from the book? And perhaps you can give us the page, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I want you to make it impossible for my time to be taken away from me. So it's not the book at all. It is its various positions. Thirdly, whoever does not believe that these positions are not contained in this book can check it out. And whoever is bothered by this can consider this to be my positions, that I am double-checking by putting questions to this witness. It's all the same to me. So I am asking you whether it's true that the KLA enjoyed unequivocal support of the West.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It isn't true, no. We didn't go there to support the KLA. We went there to stop a bad situation from getting worse, and to try to make it better, and eventually to hold an election.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When NATO got involved in the conflict by clearly taking a position against the Serbs by turning its potential only against the Serbs by threatening, and did this make it true that the KLA had the largest military alliances, their allies in order to achieve their objectives? Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not how NATO saw what it was doing, although I hesitate to speak for NATO because at the time I was not serving with NATO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you notice that the American President, on the 24th of March, 1999, in his speech to the American people, put in the very first place not the humanitarian catastrophe but the reliability of NATO?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not something the witness can deal with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a generally known fact. I'm asking him whether he noted that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can give evidence about it in due course.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was Clinton's public appearance, and it's very easy to put that into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Also, are you aware that the same thing was said by Clark on CBS news in May 2001, the 15th of May, 2001, inter alia [In English] "What Milosevic never really understood was this wasn't a conflict strictly about Kosovo. It wasn't even a conflict ultimately about ethnic cleansing. It was a battle about the future of NATO, about the credibility of the United States as a force in world affairs."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Are you asking the witness whether he can shed any light on that? Is that what you want to know?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I'm saying does this, in his opinion, reveal the background and the true reasons for the aggression against Yugoslavia. And his mission served the same function. That's my question.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I think what we were there to do was to prevent a humanitarian disaster, and I thought that at the time, and I still think it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since a number of verifiers obviously did not share your views, is this correct, this what the Italian verifiers said, and what was published in the geostrategic review called Limas in which it says that the Americans sabotaged the OSCE mission and also a quotation is made. So this is Limas, an Italian geostrategic review. These are Italian verifiers as well. [In English] "In my view, he had two primary aims. One was to infiltrate personnel into the theatre with intelligence tasks and for special forces activities, preparatory work for a predetermined war." [Interpretation] I'm waiting for the interpretation to finish. [In English] "The other was to give the war the impression that everything had been tried and thus create grounds for public consent to the aggression we perpetrated." [Interpretation] Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would certainly say that we did try everything. We certainly were not there to infiltrate people into the theatre with intelligence tasks and for special forces activities, no. We were there to carry out the task according to the agreement, in the best way we could, imperfect though it was, and without the cooperation of many of the people on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Italians say in this same source material: [In English] "Criticise Walker and his British chief of operation, Karol John Drewienkiewicz for ejecting any cooperation with Serb authorities." [Interpretation] Is that correct or not? Did they criticise you? Did individual members of the mission criticise you or did they criticise you amongst themselves without you knowing about it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can recall moments when everybody was not absolutely convinced that -- of a particular course of action. At that point, the decision was made by the head of mission, and we got on with it. It was not a popularity contest. It was a mission to try to stop bad things from happening. And if in doing that occasionally a nose got put out of joint because somebody was told, "We have heard all of the opinions, now, let's get on with the decision that the head of mission has given us," maybe occasionally, yes, noses got put out of joint, but we were there to be effective. We were not there for a beauty contest.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they also say that they criticised you, and they say here, this is a direct quote [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... to human rights. For controlling the mission's information flow, and most serious of all, for using the mission to make contacts with UCK rebels and train them to guide NATO to targets in the subsequent bombing." [Interpretation] Is this correct or not? This is what the members Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of your mission have said.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly part of our role to make contact with the KLA, so that when an incident occurred, we could talk to both sides of the incident in order to, first, find out the rights and wrongs of it, and secondly, to try to calm the situation down. You can only do that if you have access to the KLA as well as the Serb security forces. So yes, we did do that. We were not doing it in order to train the rebels. There were moments, I have to say, when in discussing events with the senior Serb officers I attempted to train them in explaining the difference between proportionate response and disproportionate response, but I didn't seem to make much progress in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this, they said that some members of the commission trained the KLA to guide the NATO bombers to various targets. The Italian verifies says, [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... bombing began on March 24, Serb security forces set out to root out all suspected UCK indicators. These operations are very probably at the heart of what NATO has described as ethnic cleansing."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So what is the question?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My question is whether this is correct, but I haven't finished.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... testified to a low level of violence as well as UCK provocation." [Interpretation] Is this correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: By March the 24th, we were in -- in Macedonia, and our only contact with what was going on in Kosovo was from people who left Kosovo after we had left, and we met them and they told us what was happening, and as I have mentioned, some satellite phone communications primarily with the KLA in which we were given information of other human rights abuses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is this correct, what the Italian verifiers also said: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... was an occasion -- was an occasion for Walker and the US State Department to denounce the Serbs for breaking the truce. Europeans saw things differently. The Albanian rebels with US encouragement versus the dramatically provoking Serb attacks in order to justify NATO coming in on their side of the conflict."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think the witness is -- the witness has dealt with this point of view. He's already given his evidence about it. So there's little point continuing on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We will get to this later, but since it is in the same place, I think that it would be useful for us to hear your opinion about this matter that the Italian verifiers have also referred to. Very briefly, this is an opinion of a relatively brief description of something that we shall get to later. [In English] "In January, Walker settled the score with his European critics by bringing the world media over to this side -- to his side. This was the political significance of the famous Racak massacre. On January 15, Serb police had carried out a pre-announced operation accompanied by observers and television cameras against UCK killers believed to be hiding out in the village of Racak. As the Serbs swept into the village, the UCK gunmen took refuge, took refuge on surrounding high ground and began firing on police, as TV footage showed. But the Serbs sent forces around behind them and many UCK forces were trapped and shot. After the Serb forces withdrew that afternoon, the UCK again took control of the village, and it was the KLA who led Walker into the village the next day to see what they describe as victims of massacre. It may be, as Serb authorities claimed and many Europeans tended to believe that the victims were in fact killed in the shootout reported by police and then aligned to give the appearance of a mass execution or massacre. In any case, the extremely emotional --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the witness is here to answer questions and not to listen to long quotations.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, for Judge May.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In order that the matter can clearly be dealt with, he should be asked about the various parts of these allegations. It's, first of all, suggested that the Serb police carried out a pre-announced operation. Just one moment. Do you know anything about that, General?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. It was certainly the case that in this area, it was stated that there will be an operation against whoever carried it out. We will find the people who did it, and we will deal with them. I remember General Loncar saying this to me in the same meeting in which he got the phone call which told him that three policemen had been killed. At the time, I said I was extremely sorry to hear of the loss of his policemen. It was certainly pre-announced. What was not announced was precisely where, when, and at what level the operation was carried out. But that was rarely given to us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Was the firing between KLA gunmen and the Serb forces?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There was a -- I believe there was a KLA presence on the outskirts of the village when the attack started on Racak, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did the KLA lead Walker into the village, as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The KLA were in the village when we got there on the Saturday morning with Walker, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Did they, as far as you could see, lead him into the village? That's what's alleged.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. They were in the village, and we went into the village. We were perfectly capable of getting in there ourselves.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic, what is the rest of the quotation?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think in view of everything that I've just said that it would be a correct assessment, which is something that the Italian verifiers are talking about precisely, that this kind of conduct on the part of Walker, [In English] "Impossible pretense of the OSCE mission." [Interpretation] Therefore, that conduct put to an end all pretenses of neutrality on the part of your mission?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not the way we saw it. We saw the Racak operation as being hugely disproportionate in view of the degree of force that was used. And further, we sincerely believed that the way we found the bodies in the gully on the hillside was the way they had been left when they had been killed. We saw no evidence of having moved bodies around or having jumbled them up to make it look as if they had been brought -- they had been killed there whereas -- instead of them having been killed elsewhere and brought together. We saw no evidence whatsoever of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll get back to Racak later on. But I'm interested in your opinion, your opinion about -- how shall I put it? -- a brief, a short assessment of this whole mission of yours which, according to the Italian verifiers, was as follows: [In English] "[Previous translation continues]... of international missions, it would be hard to find such a chaotic and tragically ambiguous enterprise." [Interpretation] Do you agree with that assessment?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly ambitious, and because no preparations had been made for it before the mission was authorised, it was extremely confusing when the mission was being started up. It was chaotic, and it was my job to get order out of chaos, and I did that to the best of my ability with some very able subordinates.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you start coming up meeting the commanders and the heads of the KLA terrorist groups?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first time I crossed into a KLA position was on the afternoon of December the 25th, 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: After that, were your meetings frequent or how frequent were they, your meeting with them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My meetings with them were not frequent. I used liaison officers to communicate with them wherever possible. I suppose I went into KLA positions between six and eight times in the course of the mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A total of eight times in the course of your mission. That was of the most number of times you talked to the KLA, is that it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the most time I talked face-to-face with them. I had many, many discussions with my liaison officers about what their attitudes were and about what they might do next. And so I don't think that was the only contact I had with them. I had a lot of contact with them, but usually through my liaison officers, who because they were assigned to deal with the KLA permanently were better able to -- to establish a working relationship with the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about Walker? Did he have daily contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How frequently did he have contacts with them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhat less than me, I would say. So if I -- if I went into KLA positions between six and eight times, he probably went in four to six times, I would think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Not counting Racak or counting Racak? Which?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not counting Racak, but you can add that to both, I suppose.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what did you talk about when you met?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We normally went in with a specific purpose such as to bring the eight VJ soldiers back. And we went in and discussed that matter which was the pressing matter at hand. We didn't engage very much in philosophical discussions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means, in fact, that you had meetings when there were crisis situations, to discuss them, such as the taking of prisoners and arresting soldiers and so on. But apart from those situations of crisis, what did your talks have to do with?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: From the end of December, we were -- we felt that we were in a fairly permanent crisis in that no sooner did one incident die down when another incident blew up. We only got the eight Serb soldiers off the top of the hill at Stari Trg on the Wednesday and Racak happened on the Friday. There wasn't much let-up between incidents to contemplate our navels.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That -- so in practical terms, that would mean that you only discussed crisis issues and incidents and nothing else when you had your contacts with the KLA, yes or no?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was how it came to work out as far as I was concerned. I always went -- I only went into a KLA location if there was something I needed to go in about. I didn't make a habit of going in to socialise.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you receive reports on incident situations -- incidents and situations of this kind? Not you personally, I mean the mission itself. When incidents occurred, did you get information from the Serb and other non-Albanian inhabitants?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, to a degree. We got information from anybody who was prepared to give us information and then we compared all different the information, looked at where it had come from, and made a judgement as to what had probably happened in reality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the complaints and reports with respect to kidnappings, violations of human rights, violence that the KLA undertook. Did you receive reports and complaints from the Serb and other non-Serb population about that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what was usually the subject of those complaints and reports?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The subject varied, but it was normally about ceasefire breaches or allegations of bad behaviour by one side or the other. We attempted to -- to record this and to try to find out what had actually happened. And if it was possible to come to a conclusion on which side the violation lay, then we made that judgement. It was not always possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did the families complain to you of people who had been kidnapped and killed, for example?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you -- how do you mean both sides? The police didn't kidnap anybody, but it was the KLA that did the kidnapping. Now, did you do anything to have those kidnapped people returned, the people who had been taken? Did you undertake an investigation or make any attempt to do so except for these eight soldiers, apart from them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we did actually get some other people back. And on the day that the nine -- the nine KLA who had been held captive, who had been captured in the border ambush, when we handed them back over to the KLA, we also took delivery of five kidnapped Serbs who we were able to return Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. to their families. That was certainly another incident that springs immediately to my mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Drewienkiewicz, do you distinguish between kidnapped civilians and terrorists seized at the border who were armed during an attempt, illegally and in armed fashion, to cross the border, those who had been arrested by the legitimate forces of a state guarding its borders? Do you make a distinction between those two? You seem to have equated them now?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that they were -- they are remembered bringing those five Serbs back. There is certainly a difference, yes. And at the time we made it clear absolutely clear that the ambush on the border was a legitimate act of the forces of a state defending its borders and it was a grave ceasefire violation by the KLA, yes. Q.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, we're going to -- Mr. Milosevic, the time has come for an adjournment. We're going to adjourn for quarter of an hour. You can go on then.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many minutes?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just to remind Your Honours, the witness is available today, having made suitable arrangements, but not, I think, beyond.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That message may not have got through, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The Court may remember that I originally said there were problems about his being here today but he reorganised things so he could be here today but not after.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, perhaps you could bring your cross-examination to a close today.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Up until what time? How long are we working for today?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are working until 12.45 -- 1.45, quarter to two, and we will have one more break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's a very short period of time. He took --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. He took over six hours. Let's see how we get on, and we'll review the position at the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you conscious of the fact that since the arrival of the mission there was a precipitant increase in the number of crimes committed by the KLA terrorist organisation?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as such, no. I don't think -- compared with when, I think, would be my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, compared to the situation before the arrival of the mission. That's what I'm comparing it to, because it was almost at zero level before the mission's arrival, their activities or, rather, the crimes that they perpetrated. And statistics show just how much this was increased very suddenly under the mission's protection. Are you aware of those facts?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as you state them, because one of the things we kept asking for was a baseline for all of this sort of stuff, and it was consistently not produced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was this schematic, that is to say, that they escalated with their crimes legitimately and that the security forces were legitimate in reacting, and then the mission accused the Serbian security forces according to a cliche, that is to say, that they used excessive use of force. Was that the general plan and schematic?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not how we saw it. The KLA, when we arrived, had stated that they would observe a ceasefire. As I have mentioned, we had wanted a firmer agreement with the Albanian side generally, but that was not forthcoming. But there was the declaration of a ceasefire, and at the start, that -- that was held to a degree. However, there were certainly cases of individual incidents involving the KLA which we deplored, but we understood that an insurgent organisation cannot be as disciplined and be able to get orders down to its -- its people, as quickly as a government set of security forces which have got much better chains of command and a proper code. There aren't codes for insurgents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many times did you go to Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, I think probably once.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you meet their chiefs on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I went there in order to discuss how we were going to get them to Rambouillet, because we had to get them onto an aircraft in order to go to Rambouillet to be part of the Albanian delegation, the Kosovo Albanian delegation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that Dragobilje was the centre of their main chiefs?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They met in different locations from time to time. That was the location that I went to in order to meet them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have your own substation there, if I can put it that way, or one of your permanent offices there?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: One of my -- we had a liaison officer there all the time with the KLA, or just about all of the time, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about KDOM? Did it have its station there too?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I assume by that you're referring to the US KDOM, which is the one that stayed in being all of the time, and I think they were there from time to time, but I'm not aware they had a permanent presence there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But your presence was permanent; is that right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was pretty permanent. The liaison officer came out from time to time to talk to me or to other people, but their -- it was the intention that there was always one of my people there for the KLA to talk to if they needed to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the presence of your representatives? Was that there to protect the chiefs of this terrorist organisation? Is that why they were there, the chiefs in Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. They were -- seemed quite capable of looking after themselves, and I don't think our presence as unarmed people in largely soft-skinned vehicles acted as -- as any protection, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was Walker in Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was not with me when I went, but I know he went there on at least one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whom you met at the time? Could you give us the names of the people you met, and the names of the people he met?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could not without going back to my notebooks. The people that I met were the people, who at the time, were the three people at the top of the KLA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were their names?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to check my books because I can't remember them offhand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you haven't got them with you, I assume.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm afraid not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who did you talk to about your impressions after touring Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: My impressions, well, I would have talked to Walker and to Keller, the head and the deputy head of the mission, because at the time, we were very concerned about ensuring that the -- the designated people were facilitated in their journey to Rambouillet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, it is common knowledge who the people were in Rambouillet. Were they the same people that you talked to in Dragobilje?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were among the people who went to Rambouillet, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you have any contacts with the families of the abducted Serbs, the members of those families?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not personally, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And when you talked to the heads of the terrorist organisations in Dragobilje, did you do anything to have them return the citizens that they had seized?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, the moment at which I went to Dragobilje was after the five Serbs were returned to their families. When I went to Dragobilje it was February, and we brought the five elderly Serbs back in late January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the representatives of the mission whom you say contacted the families of the abducted Serbs? Did they take on any responsibilities towards those families vis-a-vis those families? Did they make any promises to them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were meetings from time to time between members of the KVM and the families of the missing Serbs and indeed families of missing Albanian civilians as well, and that was quite a regular feature. It was not done by me. It was done by another part of the mission. But I was aware that it was going on. And it was obviously a cause of concern that abducted people were returned on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you score any results except for those five that you've just mentioned?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think there was one other, but I can't remember it precisely because I wasn't involved in it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did they tell you that Glodjan Dragobilje was the biggest prisons for abducted Serbs and Albanians?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you know that the abducted civilians were taken to the KLA headquarters in the village of Glodjani?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that they were subjected to torture and then killed and thrown into the canal which supplies water for Lake Radonic?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that there is detailed photo documentation and reports on those crimes?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He doesn't know. He can't answer it.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that no plan existed to expel Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I was in the Kosovo Verification Mission until we evacuated the mission on the 20th of March, I was not aware of a plan to expel the Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Does that mean that you saw nothing and heard nothing that would indicate the existence of such a plan?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw no plan. Nobody talked to me about a plan. The behaviour of some of your security forces was not always compatible with wanting them to stay in the location that they were, however.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And were you aware that the security forces never acted against terrorists when they were in groups together with civilians?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that was not my impression. My impression was that your security forces were quite prepared to go against groups of the KLA when they -- there were civilians present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But even American representatives, during 1998, were fully aware of the fact that action was not taken in those places where there was a danger of having civilians harmed. Were you aware of that fact, that no action was taken where civilians could have been harmed? Yes, no?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that Serb representatives at the meeting with your mission on the 4th of December, 1998, criticised the mission for not having started verification and that they requested that the process be initiated immediately?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. And we could have got going a lot quicker if we'd had a lot more cooperation from your people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you think that the fault for a lack of cooperation is exclusively on the side of the Yugoslav authorities?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Put like that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that on that occasion, the representatives of Serbian Yugoslavia, or, rather, the representatives of the authorities requested that the ceasefire violations of the KLA be discussed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was probably -- that was probably among the discussions, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that you did not want to discuss that on that occasion?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that. That was not the main thrust of that particular meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you. You speak about that on page 14, paragraph 3 of your statement with regard to both of these questions that I've just put to you. On that occasion, were the areas that caused concern indicated?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The areas that were causing us concern were the fact that we were Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. not being helped to build up the mission quickly, that bureaucratic procedures were being used to slow down the entry of the mission into Kosovo and its build-up. And the main purpose of the meeting, as I recall it, was to ask for assistance in speeding up the various bureaucratic procedures so that we could hire buildings and get visas issues far more quickly than was happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, did you obtain the faster issuing of visas?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It never got particularly fast, no. We actually asked if a suboffice of the visa section could be located down in Pristina so that the passports did not have to be carried physically from Pristina to Belgrade and back and that was never -- that was never put into action. So passports always had to be sent all the way up to Belgrade and all the way back, and it took many days to get visas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How many days was it actually?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depended, but it was never fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But how many days?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that my visa, to go from a single-entry visa to a multiple-entry visa, I believe it took six working days for my passport to be moved up to Belgrade, to be stamped and to come back. But that's only my recollection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But all that time you were in Kosovo. That is not being denied.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But the other place that visas were being issued very slowly was that verifiers who were being called forward to the mission were being -- were in their own countries, were going to the Yugoslav embassy in that country, and it was taking on average two weeks to get a visa from the Yugoslav embassy in that country. So they were slowed down from coming into the country. Once people were in Kosovo, if they needed to go down to Macedonia, for instance, to meet the next lot of verifiers to arrive at Skopje airport, then this was not possible if you only had a single-entry visa. So it complicated the life of the mission. It made us less effective than we otherwise would have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you bear in mind the fact that in Vienna, where the OSCE headquarters are, there was a possibility for members of your mission to obtain visas in an express manner, so to speak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, but then the mission did not all come through Vienna. They came directly from their country of origin to Skopje and from there up to Kosovo. There was no reason for them to go via Vienna.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you did have 1.300 members of your mission who had visas nevertheless, and I imagine that the difference, the remainder up to 2.000, was not due to the fact that they could not obtain visas.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: By March, the strength of the mission had gone up to 1.379, that is correct. From Christmas until March, the mission gained strength at a rate of about a hundred a week. We had hoped we would get it up to 2.000 by April.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Why was it so slow?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was fast by the standards of missions like this that are built one person at a time. It took the same amount of time for the United Nations' mission in Kosovo to build up to a similar strength when they came in in June. It basically took them about the same amount of time to get to 1.300 strong. It is a fact of life that when you're calling for people individually, then you have to have 1.300 sets of negotiations with the people and look at their curriculum vitae, call them forward. There aren't formed units of these people waiting to -- to come forward in the way that a military unit would do so with all its equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If the same time was required for the United Nations, after the 10th of June, just as you needed during the Verification Mission and the 1st that I mentioned did not require any visas, in view of their arrival in Kosovo, that practically means that visas had no effect whatsoever in terms of the speeding up or slowing down of the entire process; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come that the same time was required for the United Nations when they did not have any problems with visas, the problems that you have been indicating that you allegedly had them.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not allegedly have them, I did have them. I think you would need to compare the manning lists. The United Nations mission certainly was built up at about the same rate. However, they required a greater number of policemen in their mission, and policemen are even harder to get than the people we were getting. We did not have any many policemen in our mission, because again, they're not standing around waiting to be called forward.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And on the occasion of the meeting that you had with the Yugoslav representatives, did they indicate to you that on the road between Pec and the area up near Nis there is KLA gunfire and that Malisevo was abandoned by the population because of KLA activities and that the KLA was not exercising restraint? Did they point out all these elements to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The road between Pec and Nis is about 150 miles long, as I recall it. So I would need more precision in that question. The discussion of what was going on in Malisevo certainly happened; Malisevo was a hot spot at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But is it correct that at the meeting that was held between the representatives of the Yugoslav government with you and Walker on the 9th of December, that they asked that the KVM stop supporting the KLA and that they ask that the international community stop giving financial support to the KLA from banking sources in the West?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that allegation being made, and I remember Ambassador Walker rebutting it very, very sternly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you think that he rebutted it with good reason when it is known that through banking channels from the West, money was being earmarked for the KLA? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am really not aware of the sources of funding of the KLA, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
