utterances.text: Is it correct that the Yugoslav army called the KVM to come and carry out an inspection with regard to ceasefire violations to the east of Prizren on the border on the 14th of December when some terrorists got killed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but it was to the west of Prizren.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And was it confirmed to you then by your own patrols that there had been fighting and that large quantities of equipment had been found?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that this was a long column of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We believe it was about 145 strong.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that the KVM got approval to visit the imprisoned KLA members, those who were taken prisoner during that incident, that is?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very much later, yes. At the time that these -- that the nine prisoners were taken prisoner, that was, as you say, mid-December. As I recall it, it was the end of the first week or the beginning of the second week of January when we were granted access to these prisoners in Nis, and that was in the context of the negotiations to get the -- your eight soldiers off the hill at Stari Trg where they were being held prisoner.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that these prisoners, during the visit of Ciaglinski, your associate to the prison in Nis, told him that this was a KLA column for reinforcements and precisely this bit of information, that it was 145 members of the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. You'll be able to ask him when he appears, but that was certainly what he reported back to me, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that then they stated that they had been mobilised into the KLA against their own will, and then they went to Albania where they were trained?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That is my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that all of them during the conflict, the clash on the 14th of December, that they were all armed?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot say that, but most of them appear to have been armed, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct that -- that terrorists killed, on the 14th of December, some young Serbs in the Cafe Panda in Pec?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a killing in the Panda Bar in Pec, and some Serb youths were killed. And we never really worked out who to attribute those killings to. There was no clear evidence in either direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that the terrorists who committed this, who carried out this attack, escaped to Kapemice, that part of town which was practically a hotbed of the KLA in that town?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- I never heard that before, and I was not aware of any effective police follow-up that might have found that out either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to all their reports, all the traces led in that direction. Did you know about that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness said he wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the other side was questioning you, they said that four young men were killed. However, six young men were killed, if you remember. Do you remember even Obradovic, a high school student was killed, Vuleta, Glozdenovic, also a student. Zoran Stankovic, also a pupil. Dragan Trifkovic, also a pupil. Svet Ristic, pupil. Ivan Radovic, a university student. And the father of Ivan Radovic, Bogdan Radovic, was kidnapped. His mother and grandmother were beaten up by KLA terrorists.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: One thing at a time. General, can you help any more about this incident?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I cannot remember precisely how many people were killed in the Panda Bar attack. I believe that a number were killed outright and some died later, and it was between four and six. I can certainly remember that. I mean, it was an extremely unfortunate incident. We were not able to come to any conclusions as to the motives behind it, and nobody ever claimed responsibility for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The very fact that the perpetrators fled, and along parallel lines, one of the killed had his father abducted, and I read this out to you. He had previously been head of the municipal committee of Pec, does that sufficiently speak of how absurd and monstrous it is to claim that anybody but the KLA could have done this?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, because there have been some quite well-documented incidents elsewhere within the Balkan theatre of incidents looking like one thing and turning into another, and that was why we never ascribed blame or culpability without going into it in some detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know whose speciality this was, to create victims on their own side in order to accuse the other side of having done it, both in Bosnia and in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I can recall grenade attacks on Albanian properties, as well as against Serb properties during the time I was in Kosovo. So neither side had a monopoly of these events, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you remember that in Bosnia this was standing practice with that well-known event of the alleged shelling of the bread line in Sarajevo, the alleged --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This goes beyond the realm of the witness's evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it correct that at the meeting with the KVM on the 15th of December, the representatives of the government brought up an accusation, that the KLA was being supplied from America by some special weapons because the members of the KLA had been found to have a number of such weapons?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I recall that allegation being made, and again I recall it being refuted vigorously by Ambassador Walker.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Floren Krasniqi, an Albanian from New York involved in the construction business, and one of the main financiers of the KLA, described how certain weapons were exported from America thanks to the fact that these exports were actually being sent to hunting societies in Albania? Do you know of that confirmation of what you say that Walker refuted?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but I can observe that most of the weapons that I saw in the hands of the KLA were Kalashnikovs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about Kalashnikovs here. We're talking about special weapons that had been imported from America. You know nothing about this then; right?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of it, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct that at the meeting with the representatives of the MUP you had suggested that the number of forces be decreased and that they could not accept that because they were concerned about the security and safety of their own men? Did that seem logical to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was in connection with the -- the police garrison at Malisevo, which we were convinced was an impediment to the inhabitants Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. coming back to Malisevo because the police presence was so heavy. And we established a permanent presence of the KVM in Malisevo, and I then went to the police chief and suggested that he reduce the presence there because we felt it was threatening. It was not like a normal police station. It was more like a fort under siege with armoured cars outside of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware -- actually, this question pertains to this specialty of the KLA to kill their own people and then accuse the other side of having done it. Are you aware that there is a witness of the Prosecution, not somebody that I have brought up, somebody that they had brought up, anyway, this person says that at places where there were not police attacks that they organised their own attacks against peaceful villages. Are you aware of this practice?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no, because if we had been aware of it, we would have commented on it publicly. When you find a naked dead body by the road at 8.00 in the morning, it's very difficult to work out who killed him or her.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am talking about a protected witness for the Prosecution who asserts that they organised attacks of their own against peaceful villages and that these were --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has dealt with this. He has given his evidence about it as far as he can. Now, move on to another topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that is the subject. Jako Krasniqi, Hashim Thaci, Sulejman Selimi, and Rexhep Selimi organised an entire series of killings of Albanians, especially those --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is what you say. The witness has given his answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am asking him not about what I am saying but about what I have been reading from the statement of this protected witness. He is a protected witness because he is an Albanian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. Now, let us -- Mr. Milosevic, the cross-examination is to put things to the witness, not for argument. Now, you've asked him about this practice, as you allege, and he has said what he can about it. There's no point going on putting other things to him.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] However, I'm asking whether it is logical for the executive chief of the Verification Mission to know or not to know about the multitude of these crimes that were committed by this groups headed by Thaci, Krasniqi, Selimi, and others. So this question directly has to do with what he was duty-bound to monitor and report on, and it has to do with the testimony of your witness here, the Prosecution witness, not something that I have been saying just off-the-cuff. I am asking him questions related to the subject matter that he was actually dealing with in Kosovo. That's what he was there for. And you have the same thing --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask him about the practice that you put forward. Now, is there something else you want to ask him about?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do not understand your question. Of course I want to ask him about a great many things, but it seems to me that this is a very important qualification of carrying out a series of crimes against Albanians, where they had a personal interest of their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Now, the question is do you know of attacks on Albanians, as I understand it, by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As such, sir, no. There were a -- there was a series of killings which went on throughout January and early February, which ran at the rate of about four a week, and we were not able to find out who was carrying them out and neither was the Serbian police who were there in considerable numbers and had rather better access to forensic science than we had with our people.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: So it's -- so that it's clear, this is killings of Albanians?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was killings of Albanians and of Serbs. Both groups were involved, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I understand this -- I do not understand, rather, this need to strike a balance between criminals and the other side all the time, but anyway, do you know about this particular case when a group headed by Hashim Thaci beat up Luzer Buhara [phoen] from Cerovik who worked as a traffic policeman in Pristina? They burned his house down. And then Thaci used a knife to draw various symbols on his chest, to carve them. All of this is dealt with in the testimony of this Albanian witness. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this same Hashim Thaci who carved symbols on the chest of Albanians, do you know his photograph with Madeleine Albright and Clark and Blair taken together with this group?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: This is all a matter of general comment. It's not for this witness to deal with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And can he answer a question of ethics? Clark, Albright, Blair and others taking photographs with him, can that be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No. It's not for him to answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I'll skip over many questions because it seems that I will not have enough time once again to ask everything I want to ask.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that when the soldiers were exchanged they had noticeable signs of abuse, of maltreatment, and physical mistreatment on them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. They had definitely been beaten up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that revolted citizens set up barricades throughout Kosovo at the time to protest against the fact that the state wasn't taking more energetic measures to combat terrorism when it was allowing things of this kind to happen at all?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that barricades were set up. They looked more like paramilitaries to me because they were wearing black ski masks to hide their faces, and they were carrying long-barrelled weapons in public. I was surprised that the police did not do something about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What they looked like to you is one question and whether they were civilians is another question. Do you consider that they were civilians or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were dressed in -- generally in black leather jackets, and they could have been civilians or they could have been off-duty members of the security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know, just as an aside, of the orders -- are you aware of the orders to the effect that each unit in Kosovo was duty-bound immediately to disarm and take into custody any kind of paramilitary unit in its area of responsibility? Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't, and it certainly did not happen that day, which I think was the 6th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what day it happened. What I'm asking you is whether you were aware of an order issued to that effect and that it was respected and acted upon?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of the order. It was certainly not being respected and acted on when I personally encountered these paramilitaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You insist on saying that they weren't citizens but that they were paramilitary formations, is that right, paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They looked like paramilitaries to me. They worked as a group, and they gave orders to the civilians who were bystanders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that on the 15th of January, in the Decani area, a member of the Verification Mission was wounded?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two members of the Verification Mission were wounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm talking about, two members.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Two members, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that on that day KVM vehicles were led by two MUP vehicles and that the KLA opened fire and wounded two representatives of the international people and wounded a local man too?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is certainty the case that the KVM vehicles were in the same general area as the MUP vehicles. It is my recollection that the KVM vehicles were leading the MUP vehicles. And it's certainly true that we later discovered it was the KLA who had carried out the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But what was quite obvious, that is that the column was targeted in which there were MUP vehicles too, was that not sufficient for you to observe that this was in fact being done by the KLA?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I was very concerned that it was a come-on and that Serbian police might well have carried out the shooting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you assume that the Serb police shot at the column in which there were members of the Serb police, is that it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because the two sets of vehicles were quite separated. I think there were between 50 and 100 yards between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that means only direct recognition by the KLA could finally change your judgement. That is to say that it wasn't the Serb police, that the Serb police were innocent victims being innocently accused.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: After this incident, I discussed with the people who came under fire, one of whom is Richard Ciaglinski, and having spoken to as many people as I could who were there on the ground in the incident, I drew my conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So ultimately only after direct recognition by the KLA did you put away any doubt that had fallen on the Serb police force as suspects.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I recall it, I spoke to everybody who had taken part in this incident, and when I reviewed everything, which by this stage was 2.00 in the morning, I concluded that I didn't know who had done it, but the balance of probability pointed at a come-on by the MUP. Simultaneously, we were asking our people who were with the KLA to get to the KLA commander and to ask him his version of the event. In the course of the next day, I was told by my people with the KLA that the KLA had admitted it was their people who had done it. We then encouraged them to own up to this. They declined and so we then stated in a press statement that it had been done by the KLA who had admitted it. That was the sequence of events.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What about the sequence of events? Does it not lead you to conclude or at least lead others to conclude the criteria which you use to base your judgements and conclusions on and that you always assume that it must be the Serbs who are at fault, regardless of what happens --

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- the Serbs were to blame?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That was not my judgement. My judgement at the time was based not only on what had happened when the firing took place but what had happened during the earlier part of the day when there'd been quite a lot of talking between my verifiers and the Serb police who were very adamant that we should not go forward with them when they went. And it was in fact to change over the garrison of a location that they went forward. And we were going with them to make sure that the garrison was changed over and not reinforced. But it was based on all of those conversations that took place and were reported to me, and the circumstances of the shooting, that I concluded at the time that the balance of probability was that the Serbs had shot at my verifiers. That was my judgement then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. The reasons are clear and -- why you changed them later on. Is it true on the 15th of January - that is my next question - that you sent Maisonneuve to Racak, the Stimlje municipality?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also correct that on the 15th of January, the inhabitants of Racak told him that there were a number, not many, of people who had been killed and arrested and several wounded?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was what he was told by the people who were -- whom he met as dark was falling that Friday afternoon. The situation was very confused at the time, and he perceived the priority then as evacuating the wounding, which is what he did. There were also unconfirmed reports that a number of men had been taken away by the police, but they were unconfirmed at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but that was a discussion with the inhabitants of Racak that he had and the report that he tabled to you.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. But you have to remember that those people had spent the afternoon in their houses under fire, not exactly able to congregate in the streets and to find out precisely what was going on. Each person was giving his or her view of what they had seen from their very limited standpoint.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you make a selection of those statements, statements about that according to a criteria of how the Serbs -- what the Serbs could be Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. blamed for and what they could not be blamed for? Because according to what Maisonneuve said, there was no foundations for an accusation against the Serbs, of blaming the Serb security forces for what had happened.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall Maisonneuve making any comment like that, but all of the reports from that period have been produced as -- as evidence and are available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We know what those reports were like. And is it true that in Racak you came one day later, that is to say on the 16th, together with Walker, and that you found members of the KLA there?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it also true that the members of the KLA would not allow you to leave Racak without having a meeting with Walker?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it also true that Walker surprised you when he condemned the FRY government and attributed the blame to that government for what had happened in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was surprised at the time that he was as specific as to refer to the event as a massacre. However, I do agree with what he said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you agree, how could he have surprised you then?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because it was in the middle of a press conference and we had not discussed this before the event. It came out, as I recall, as an answer to a question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know that Hashim Thaci, in an interview to the BBC on the 24th of March, 2000 said the following and I quote, "That a unit of the KLA was active in Racak and that many members of the KLA courageously died in fighting the Yugoslav forces."

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've got no doubt that the KLA may well have been present in Racak, but I never saw that as a justification for flattening the place with artillery.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was Racak flattened when you arrived on the scene in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was considerable damage to many of the houses, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, can you then use the term "flattened", if that's what happened?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was certainly attacked with artillery and heavy-calibre weapons in a way that was inappropriate to counter an insurgent operation in my view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But there is proof that that is not correct, that the artillery was used, that that is incorrect.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. Now, do you know that on the Internet you can find a statement by Madelaine Albright given to the BBC and she says that preparations were necessary for the incident in Racak and that the fans were flamed in order to exert pressure on the European allies in order to effect military intervention.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You must ask her about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm asking you, whether you were aware of it, whether you knew anything about a statement to that effect.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not as stated like that, and I do not necessarily agree with it seeing it now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: However, this belated recognition of the US Minister reminds us of a statement made --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not a proper question. That's a comment by you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask the proper question?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know of a statement made by the vice-president of the parliamentary Assembly of the OSCE, the German, Wimmer, a rare European dignitary who did not think that the TV massacre was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That sounds like another comment by you. Just ask the question. What is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Are you aware of the statement made by the vice-president of the parliamentary Assembly of the OSCE which states as follows, "We refute the manipulations being carried out by the television footage with the intention of provoking a NATO intervention in Kosovo or everything would point to the creation of certain reactions so when I see certain images and photographs, we -- it makes us issue automatic orders to our soldiers."

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the accused please slow down when reading.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're asked to slow down. You're asked to slow down when reading. General, can you help with this? First of all, do you know about this statement?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know this particular diplomat. I know he wasn't on that hillside with me, and I know what I saw on that hillside, and it was not manipulation by the media. It was dead men who had been gunned down in cold blood, as far as I was concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know the assertion that those people had been brought there, because you and Walker arrived when the village was already under KLA control. You arrived 16 hours after their entrance into the village, and the time -- and this meantime when they could have done everything. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware that there was a lapse which -- of which most was night-time when we were not there, before we got there. I do not believe that the KLA manipulated this -- this scene so that you would -- your forces would get the blame. I believe what we saw was what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in Racak the members of the so-called 121st brigade were present, Agim Selak and, or rather the Sadik Salja Battalion, and that's where the head of the Nerodim Operative Zone was in the house of Nosti Mikmeki [phoen]. Are you aware of that? That was precisely in Racak.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you happen to know that up until the 15th of January, the members of the KLA terrorists in the Racak area had killed a policeman Sinisa Mihajlovic, Nazmija Aluri, Svetislav Pesic, Sasa Jankovic, Ranko Djordjevic, and then some civilians, Mista Seli [phoen], and Enver Gashi? And before that, in November, that they had set fire to Dzema Batica's house in Racak. And later on, immediately prior to the intervention, they killed a policeman by the name of Svetislav Pesic from an ambush several days prior to the intervention against the terrorists in Racak? Are you aware of that, of this pretext, of went before?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there was violence there before, and therefore it was the duty of your police forces to investigate the crimes properly, take evidence, arrest the people, put them on trial, and send them to jail if you find them guilty, but that was not what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you know why an investigation was not possible at the time.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of any attempt to carry out a proper police investigation before the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the fact that the investigating judge of the court in Pristina, Danica Marinkovic, a woman judge, tried on several occasions to go out and investigate in Racak but she was not able to do so because of the fighting? She had to do this three days later also on pain of gunfire?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly met her on the Sunday and offered to escort her personally into the village. She declined.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that the entire village was encircled by trenches and bunkers, that they were all round the village, and even behind the village, towards Jezerske Planine, the mountains, there was another line or row of trenches?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am aware that there was one quite long trench, probably about between 50 and 80 yards or metres long, that I walked over on my way up the hill to the gully. That was the only trench that I was aware of.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did you go round the whole village and its environs to see how many bunkers and trenches there were or did you only take note of the one you actually had to jump across, walk over?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not go looking for other trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A moment ago, we established, not very clearly though, that you were informed about this police action in advance. That is to say that the Verification Mission had been informed of this police action beforehand and that your people were present on the 15th of January, that they were in Racak.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I don't think we were informed specifically. We were informed when -- when the policemen were killed a week earlier, General Loncar said to me, "We will -- we will take action against that," yes. We very rarely were told, "There is going to be an operation at a certain place at a certain time with the following object in view." That is what we would have hoped to have received, that sort of information, so that we could then be there to make sure that no serious abuses took place. But it was very rare that that happened, and it did not happen on this occasion at Racak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But a moment ago, you confirmed by stating a name and surname that your man Maisonneuve was in Racak on the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was -- yes, he was. I sent him there at about half past two in the afternoon from Pec, and he did that because we had got reports coming in that there was firing into the village, that village and neighbouring village, by heavy calibre weapons by your forces. As a result of that, he went down to that location, which was not strictly in his area of operations, but I was very concerned that I wanted someone senior and very experienced on the spot.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. But there must have been some other verifiers with him who were in Racak on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: And they reported to him, and their report is part of the reports that have been laid before the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's the whole point, that the verifiers who were there on the 15th of January saw nothing of what you and Walker, who came later on after a pause in which the KLA brought in the bodies and put them in that gully, you saw nothing of that sight?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maisonneuve arrived as dusk was falling. He stayed within the village. Nobody told him that there was something to go and see up in the gully. He had no idea that such a thing had taken place. It was an area where there had been a very major firefight during the day, and I would certainly not have expected him to go wandering off into the gathering gloom on the off chance of finding something about 300 metres from the village. Which direction would he have gone in?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You've said yourself now that there was major -- a major firefight in Racak, and your statements were that the security forces had come and perpetrated a massacre over the civilians. Now tell me what happened. Was it a firefight or was it a massacre of civilians?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I think we've exhausted this topic. The witness has said everything that he can say about it. His opinion will not assist us any more, and there will be other witnesses who can give evidence about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in addition to your own verifiers who entered Racak on the 15th that there was a television crew from Associated Press.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically, no. They didn't report to us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But they published in the information media what they saw, nevertheless.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it's available.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is. Do you know that there were no civilians in the village and that the villagers, already during the summer, had left Racak because of the operations under way in the area? Except for a few exceptions, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think one of the reports that was placed before the Court last week detailed at one stage a statement of what the population of Racak was and the fact that food aid was needed for them. So, yes, we did know that some of the inhabitants of Racak had fled, but some were still there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was winter, and eyewitnesses say that there was smoke coming out of just one chimney, which was where the headquarters of the KLA was, which is where equipment was found --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness -- the witness can't deal with this.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eyewitnesses say that there was shooting all over and that the shooting stopped only around 1600 hours. Does that coincide with your own findings?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. My findings were that the shooting into Racak stopped before Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the shooting stopped that was going into all of the other villages and that because there was the sound of shooting going on, that the people in Racak did not realise that the fire had lifted in their specific area and so were very surprised to suddenly see the -- the MUP arriving in the middle of the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have here a few witnesses from Racak who are also not my witnesses but the witnesses of this false Prosecution. For example, Nesret Shabani says on the 15th of January in Racak there was a real war that was going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can -- you can deal with this with other witnesses. This witness came the next day. You can ask him about his evidence, but we're -- if going to get much further going over this ground about which he can't really answer.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this is not a witness who is merely testifying about what he had seen. He is the executive chief of the Verification Mission, and it is assumed that he knew or had reason to know the facts that were used in such a way in the war against Yugoslavia. Therefore, I do have the right to question him by invoking other witnesses, because it was his duty to collect these facts. So the question would then have to be why did he not collect these facts from these witnesses? Because he was in charge of the Verification Mission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a question he can be asked.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's why I'm putting it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The reports that were put together on the night of the 15th represented all the information we had at that moment and had obviously come from a variety of sources. Some of it was the eyewitness reports of my verifiers, some of it had been the answers to questions from them to the villages. As you have seen, the facts were not immediately apparent, and we found out more as time went on, and that is often the case. It was not a very clear situation. It was getting dark. Everyone, all of the villagers that were in the village, were very frightened and confused. There were wounded people. It was not a clear situation. We dealt with the situation that we found. We made the report as best we could. And then as we got more reports overnight, we went back, and looked again, and then saw what had not been seen the afternoon previous. Nobody attempted to cook the books, and every one of these reports is as it was written at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In connection with this selective presentation of information, both in this case and in all other cases --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a comment. We're going to -- yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is not a comment. I am putting forth a request to you. In view of your authority, you should adopt a writ of disclosure which would make it incumbent upon the American, British, French, and every other service to disclose the information they have not only about this case but other cases where things were rigged in order to accuse the Serb side for the crimes that were committed by the other side. And if you do not have the authority to order that, then you cannot be in charge of these proceedings at all, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That is a totally different matter as to disclosure, and if you have an application about it, we'll obviously consider it. Meanwhile, it's nothing to do with this witness. We'll adjourn now for another quarter of an hour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just a digression, since I checked this during the break. You said, concerning the crime in the Panda cafe when six young Serb men were killed, you said that you could not establish and you are claiming even now that you do not know who did this. In diagram DZ that you presented here on page 7, this is a chronology of events, under 44 you wrote, in relation to this crime in the Panda cafe, the attack of the KLA on the Panda cafe if Pec. Is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would need to be reminded of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have we got the tab number for the chronology?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the diagram called the chronology, but you can check that later, because I would like to save time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote, "Attack of the KLA on the Panda cafe in Pec." This is under item 44 in what you called the chronology. Diagram DZ. Now let's go back to Racak. Yesterday when you spoke about yet another event when members of the KLA were killed, you said that underneath you saw a big puddle of blood. How come you didn't see any blood in Racak at this place where this execution was allegedly carried out? How come there was not a pool of blood there when there were far more people there than in the incident that you had described yesterday?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think you are talking about the -- my description of the Rogovo killings, when a number of people had been killed inside a minibus and their blood was dripping out of the minibus into the farmyard, and it was mud and slush on the surface of the ground. At Racak, the ground is -- is not so muddy and is more sandy, as I recall it, and so there was not the same opportunity for blood to puddle. However, there was blood at the -- associated with each body that I saw at Racak, but they were not piled in one place with a non-porous surface underneath them so the blood was able to collect and run in the way that it did out of the back of the minibus. I think that's the point you're wanting me to comment on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, you did not mention at all this particular element in your description of events. So where were the casings then if that is where the execution was carried out? How come there were no casings anywhere?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were -- I looked around out to about five metres around the gully and did not find any shell casings. I did not go further out because there was brush and scrub all around, and it would have taken a long time to have gone round and examined all the way out to, say, 30 or 40 metres out, which is a range from which these people could have been killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We are going back to the statements related to Racak. A Prosecution witness says that there was a real war in Racak on that day and that the KLA was in the village on that day. This is Nesret Shabani, a witness from Racak. Also, there is a Prosecution witness Drita Emini who claims -- she claims that they had trenches, that the local villagers helped the KLA dig trenches two or three months before this alleged massacre and that they worked at night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The witness has given his evidence about the trenches. He's given his evidence about what he knows. Now, these are all matters of pure comment. The tab number for the chronology is 63 in the bundle, and the entry, number 44, is as the accused put it to the witness. Yes. Let's move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This lady witness, do you know that a witness from Racak claims that trenches had been dug at least a month before this alleged massacre, and yesterday you claimed that these were freshly dug trenches, and this applies to the part that you had skipped?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, that's a new point, freshly dug or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the evidence is the trench over which this witness stepped was newly dug. There will be other evidence about trenches as we'll see, for example, when we look at the material related to Racak, generally, perhaps the consideration of a binder in relation to that location.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was my opinion that the trench I saw was newly dug because the spoil did not have grass growing out of it, which would have done if it had been there for some time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. I asked you how come you did not know that there were witnesses who assert that three months before that they had dug trenches and that they finished them a month before that, and how could there have possibly been grass in the middle of the winter. This was the 15th of January. Grass could not grow during the winter between the 15th of December and the 15th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is the point? What's the point for the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The point is that there is a major difference involved between what the witness has been asserting and what the witnesses who are the inhabitants of Racak have been asserting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: If that is right, you could comment on it in due course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We also have Xhamajl Beqiri, a witness from Racak, who confirmed on the 15th of January in Racak, that there were members of the OSCE, that is OSCE verifiers were there. This is also a Prosecution witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You can ask the witness about it when he or she comes. We are also going to hear, are we not, from the OSCE witnesses who came here or at least one of them. Maisonneuve I believe.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you can ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of these statements of witnesses from Racak when you were collecting facts -- no? No, you don't know about it?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that this witness claims that OSCE verifiers were by Berisha's brook in Racak?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reports of that have been placed before the Court represent the facts as we knew them in Pristina that night. And as I've said before, they changed as -- as we got more facts in, our understanding of what had happened changed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Eyewitnesses say that around 1600 hours, gunfire had ceased, policemen were still in the trenches that they had taken, and after them the observers arrived, the OSCE observers, and TV crews. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not aware of it, but I have to observe that this was happening on the same afternoon that we had just taken two casualties, and the one thing we had done was put out an all stations message saying for crying out, stay back a bit. So this was not a moment at which everyone was in a race to get to the target area ahead of the police. This was a moment when everyone was perhaps holding back a bit for justifiable reasons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Witnesses claim that fighting was taking place on a two or three kilometre long front line and that there were terrorists who had been killed at several places. Did you have a report about that from your representatives who were in Racak on that day?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I recall the report saying that there was firing into villages along a two to three kilometre front line, yes. I was not aware that there had been specifically KLA members killed, otherwise it would have appeared in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware that according to the Human Rights Watch report and the reports of the journalists who were with Walker on the 16th of January, it said that many of the bodies had obviously been mutilated, their nails pulled out, et cetera. Are you aware of this kind of report, and are you aware of the fact that this was not the truth?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was aware that one corpse had been beheaded, and we never knew who did it. And certainly it was never attributed to the Serb security forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, later on it was established that all the persons killed -- it was established by all the forensic expertise carried out later that they were all killed by firearms and that the injuries to the bodies were inflicted later by animals. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I believe I recall some of that, but I believe the beheading of the one individual was actually done with an axe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this was not shown by any of the expert findings, any of the forensic findings. Do you know about what the Human Rights Watch said, that the army and police unselectively attacked civilians, burnt houses, and that they had orders to kill all the inhabitants over the age of 15? Do you think that such statements were made for those purposes, that is to Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. say, to create this kind of a sensational crime?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not for the witness to answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Christoph Shatello [phoen], a journalist of Le Monde, in his report from the scene, he said that after the Associated Press left and the police left that the OSCE mission entered in three vehicles. They found at first one killed person, one dead person, and a few wounded people. Are you aware of that? These were your observers.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That sounds like the first people arriving and, yes, that is consistent with the reports that we put together on the Friday evening in Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can't you see the discrepancy between your verifiers when there was this conflict between the KLA and the police and also the period after 1600 hours when the village was taken? What about this difference, this time difference involved between then and when you came there with Walker? Doesn't that say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went there as soon as we became aware that something really bad had happened, and that was on Saturday morning. I made that clear in my previous evidence. We were not aware that there were a large number of people up on the hillside who had been killed at any stage on Friday night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in a statement for the Canadian news this same man, Shatello, said that he arrived in Racak at about 1600 hours where he came across the police, that the operation was difficult, effective, and clean?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's clearly his view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And a cameraman belonging to Associated Press made a press statement saying that it was a crystal clear operation. He says that from the very beginning, he followed the fighting, and he has a film on -- he has footage of it which in France created --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, no good putting these to the witness. Just a moment. If you've got the footage, you can show it to us, but it's no good going on with this, asking the witness about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that Le Monde of France wrote that there was practically no civilian population in Racak, that they had fled the previous year with just a few exceptions and had not returned?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He's given his evidence about it. It doesn't matter what Le Monde says. It's this evidence we're concerned with.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about a journalist who was on the spot and who is of course an eyewitness and who says himself that he wasn't able to understand the mystery of it, the mystery that took place with Walker's statement and the alleged massacre. Do you know that eyewitnesses state that the real fighting was in fact in the forests, because members of the KLA had withdrawn to the forests above the village?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not aware of that, no, but I'm not sure it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But some questions are relevant. Some of the questions asked by journalists publicly in the information media, for example. And one such question is the following, which is interesting: How could the policemen had rallied so many men and taken them peacefully to execution, their execution, when they were under fire, because they were being shot at from all the surrounding hills. And the shooting went on the next day and the following day, when the investigating judge was shot at too?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not for the witness to say. The fact is he went there and that's his evidence, and you haven't challenged it, and he saw the corpses. That's his evidence. You haven't challenged that.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am challenging the testimony precisely now and asking how that was possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The question is: Was there any logic in somebody collecting up citizens under a whole rainfall of bullets and take them to an execution of any kind?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's not for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How about the gully next to the village that was not noted by the villagers and OSCE observers who entered the village and talked to the villagers and looked for the wounded?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was between 200 and 300 metres from the nearest house, as I recall. It was getting dark. Nobody indicated that there was anything up there that should be gone and looked at, and it was not our practice to go off-road, in the dark, at this stage. As I've previously said, we had just had two verifiers wounded. We were not going to go out into the dark on the off chance of finding something when there was no indication that there was anything to find. It would have been stupid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And does the very fact that from that time on, when nothing was found of what you found the next day, whether it is contestable that from that time when the police withdrew, at least 15 to 16 hours went by, during which time the village was under the control of the KLA while you went with Walker to find those dead?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was certainly a time lapse, yes, and I've stated what I saw, and when I saw it, and what my impression was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you consider it could be justified that three days later, Figaro from the spot published an article, "Kosovo, Doubts of a Massacre," in which he asked himself whether Ambassador Walker had been too -- too hurried in accusing the Serb security forces of having cold bloodedly ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm going to stop these questions because it doesn't matter what Figaro or anybody else says about it. What matters is what this evidence says at the time. You've heard what the witness said. He's told you what he saw and what his opinion was. Now, you can ask about that. But putting what these journalists said is of no assistance to anybody. If you want to call them, call them by all means, and we'll hear their evidence in due course. But meanwhile, we're just wasting time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, on that topic, can I just make one -- two very short points. Mr. Wladimiroff tells me that the amici do have questions they wish to ask this witness. In relation to the witness who is to be called tomorrow, there are some quite important procedural matters. They won't take more than a couple of minutes but Mr. Ryneveld would like to deal with them in a couple of minutes for everyone, not least the accused having all the material he must have for tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, Mr. Wladimiroff, one of the amici curiae, will conduct the cross-examination if there is enough time to do so. But I should like at this point in time, in view of the ongoing matters, and I'd like to refer to Rule 90 which gives you the authorisation, and I do understand this, this does come under the competency and the authority of the Court, to avoid the unnecessary wasting of time, and I'm sure you'll see to that. However, I do consider that the manner of procedure today, where it was stated in advance that this witness is at the Court's disposal only for today in some way brings you into a situation which --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Tapuskovic, we have these matters in mind, and I'm going to ask the witness if he will return, if that's what you want me to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is -- what is the point?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand, and I'm trying not to take up even a little of your time. What I want to say is that I know you are there to decide upon matters of this kind and you will do so when time is consumed unnecessarily, but when the Prosecution says in advance that somebody's going to be at the disposal of the Tribunal for only for today, that makes the problem more difficult. Now, the witness is here and it is up to you to assess. You are the ones who are to assess when his testimony is to come to an end. But if somebody states in advance that he's only here for one day, then that jumps the gun so to speak. Of course you are the ones to decide, and I completely agree with that. I just wanted to draw your attention to the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, and what we'll do is ask him at a convenient time to come back. Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't think the time for cross-examination of this witness can be limited. He is a witness who is testifying to the entire work of the mission. He has brought hundreds of pages of various documents, and during the examination-in-chief, he spent over a day and a half discussing, and these testify to who pulled the trigger during the aggression.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We agree. He is an important witness. He's given lengthy evidence. In due course we shall ask him if he can, at a convenient time, to come back. Now let's go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it is logical for us to continue the examination until we exhaust all the questions and not to have the witness return.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, my question is the following: In view of the indisputable fact after so much time had gone by from the withdrawal of the police to the arrival of the verifiers, that the KLA had the village under its control, was the KLA able to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We have been over this. You've made your point. The witness has answered as best he can, which is dealing with the matters he knows about, and he's dealt with it. Now, it sounds to me, very much, you're coming on to the matters which we will have to resolve at the end of this case, and there's no further assistance to be gained by remaking points to the witness. It's mere argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am asking him whether in his opinion the KLA could have collected up the bodies in that time lapse and could they have taken them there to that collective area where they put the bodies all together?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The only question is from what the witness saw, would it be consistent with that discussion?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was not consistent with what I saw, and that was not the impression I gained then or now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said that the verifiers were in Racak on the 15th, but before that you also said that they were not officially invited, not officially called. However, the British member of the Verification Mission, according to what he told the Guardian, because the Guardian quotes his statement, his name was Nel Strechen [phoen], he says he was officially called to go to Racak before the operation, and that was the first public recognition that the Verification Mission was -- had been previously informed about the operation in Racak. Is that correct or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And are you aware of the conclusion by the Frankfurt Arunja [phoen] of the 21st of January which cautions on the following: "Nothing would have been as fatal as the abuse of NATO --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Doesn't matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- for terrorist purposes in Kosovo."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's irrelevant what the newspaper thinks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how then is it possible that on the very next day and the day after when the teams arrived to carry out an inspection that unarmed villagers launched an attack on them? How was that possible?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you're -- I believe you're referring to the judge Marinkovic going into the village in the course of Sunday, and at that point there was a KLA presence in the village. We had spoken to them, and as I recall it, they had stated that they would allow the judge into the village without there being any violence if she came on her own, if we brought her. If a large police presence came into the village, then they would shoot at it. She chose to go into the village with a large police presence, and she got shot at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you feel -- does it seem to you that this whole thing was abused? People are saying here that I refer to the press, but Racak was abused precisely in the press to create a general atmosphere to be used as a pretext against the aggression against Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it's not a matter for this witness. These are irrelevant questions as far as his evidence is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then tell me what you think. Why Finland, the Helenna Rantov [phoen] of Finland, first gave recognition to Yugoslav pathologists and then without challenging their findings had her personal attitude of being undefined in her personal position and standpoint?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would need to ask her that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But this is not a personal question, a question addressed -- it has to do with relationships, the relationship to what happened. Why you did Ms. Rantov say she had to consult the representatives of the Foreign Ministry for her to be able to give her professional findings, to state her professional findings? What has the Foreign Ministry got to do with forensic expertise?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: That's a rhetorical question. The witness can't answer it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw the photograph of Walker with the whole team of people next -- and the Albanian next to the body with the Albanian white cap on the man's head. How is it possible for somebody to be hit in the head and have his cap remain on his head, which is like the shell on an egg? When people jump out of their shoes when they are hit in this way, whereas this man has his white cap intact on his head. Did you have in mind that this could possibly be a rigged scene for television purposes and the distribution of bodies there and how they were piled up?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was -- that certainly was one of the thoughts that went through my head as I was going up the hill. By the time I had seen the bodies and the way they were piled together, I concluded, to the best of my knowledge, that they had not been moved, that they had been killed where they lay. That was my opinion at the end of my time on the top of that hill in the gully, and it remains my opinion. And if I was a terrorist, I wouldn't go around with a white hat on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely what I'm claiming, that he didn't go around with a white hat on but that somebody placed it on his head afterwards, because forensic experts say that from a shot of that kind and a wound with that kind, your eyes would pop out let alone a cap being displaced from your head. He wasn't born with a cap on his head.

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was my view at the end of my time in that gully on that hill that those people had been killed where they lay. I did not think the bodies had been interfered with.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this movement of the bodies from the place where you saw them and transporting them to the local mosque before all the investigations had been conducted does that act present one of a series of evidences to show that the whole thing was rigged? Would that indicate that to you?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We were not entirely in charge of what was going on up on that hill. However, that was one of the reasons why we took quite so much video footage of where everyone was and what their wounds were, so that we had the best possible evidence in the circumstances that we were able to get. We didn't have on hand instantly available a forensic team to be able to bring it in and to carry out a proper scene of crime investigation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know about Thaci's statement, in addition to the one that I quoted at the beginning, that many members of the KLA had died in Racak and that Racak was a turning point for the West to become convinced of the need for military intervention?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: I haven't heard that statement specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: To bear that out, we have a statement from another KLA fighter to German television, to the effect that him and his co-fighters attacked the police intentionally in order to provoke a conflict and thus --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: There's no point asking -- there's no point asking the witness. And if you're going to try and rely on material like that, you must put it before the Trial Chamber at the proper time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How then do you explain the explanation given by Danica Marinkovic, the investigator judge from Pristina, and she is one of the best-informed people, quite obviously, into this event in Racak, who says at the very outset, "I found it rather strange, Walker's associate's behaviour rather strange, General Drewienkiewicz, who tried to prevent us from going to the crime scene." Is that true or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I said that I was very happy to go with her to the crime scene. What I did not want was to have more fighting flare up and get more people injured.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that in the minutes in the report it says that a heavy [indiscernible] 12.7 millimetre machine-gun was found, two pistols, two automatic rifles, 7.63, six of those, two sniper rifles of Chinese production, 12 mines with a hand rocket launcher, 7.820 bullets of different calibre, 3 portable radio stations, sanitary material, and uniforms with insignia. Do you know about all these items from the minutes and report?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. And at the time, we asked that a joint investigation be carried out and this sort of evidence be made available and this was never done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then do you acknowledge that the investigating court of the district court in Pristina conducts an investigation and that their report is a relevant fact to learn the truth about the events that took place? Would you acknowledge that?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only provided that the weapons produced could be linked to the deceased, which would be normal forensic practice.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's precisely what they found. They found those weapons on the spot where the deceased were. Is that contested or not?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, absolutely. At the time, I said if there are weapons, then let us see them, and let us see the evidence linking the weapons to the corpses, and this was never done. And we asked several times.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is the connection not enough, the weapons and the bodies? And in the forensic report, looking at 37 bodies when the paraffin [as interpreted] glove was taken off, that it was established that they had in fact shot from fire arms?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: This evidence was never made available to us. This is the document that was handed over to the accused this morning, so it is available. The passage that he's reading from, he's reading in the Serbian. In fact, in the English, it reads as follows: "When we arrived in the village of Racak," this is the judge's report, "I was informed by police representatives that during the search of the terrain, members of the MUP RS Ministry of the Interior of Serbia had found weapons and parts of military uniforms and they had taken everything with them." It goes on to say everything on the site was photographed. So this is an example of how the document really ought to be made available to the witness so that he can comment on it. I'll make mine available to save time and then it can go on the overhead projector if that's of assistance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Put -- it goes on the projector.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't want them to take up my time, because the Prosecutor has used -- Mr. Nice has used far more time, and I beg him not to use up my time because I have quite a few more questions to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: He is saying that the position should be made clear so that it's fair, and it's fair to the witness and it's fair to those who have to deal with this case. If it goes on the overhead projector. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So what is on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: The statement that I read says that the following weapons were found that day, and it lists a number of weapons, and there is nothing that I can see that links the people that were -- we found dead with these weapons. These weapons could have been in the basement of any police station anywhere throughout Kosovo. Every police station has got plenty of these weapons available. And so I do not believe that this specifically links the people that were killed with these weapons. And if it did, it was not a capital offence to own a weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You have placed on the ELMO precisely the passage that I read from the investigating judge's report, and the figures are the same, the numbers are the same. And do you consider that a police unit that is being shot at from the surrounding hills by members of the KLA and who are withdrawing from the village should leave heavy machine-guns and automatic rifles behind and sniper rifles behind, bombs, ammunition, and all the rest of it, at the disposal of those who will undoubtedly enter the village as soon as they leave or should they collect up all these things and take them with them?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
utterances.text: It entirely depends upon the circumstances. The fact that is being alleged is that these weapons were associated with the people that were killed, and this does not appear to carry out that association, to prove it, and nor does anything that I encountered at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That merely confirms that the OSCE observers and KLA terrorists were very well synchronised. That is without a doubt?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, that is not an appropriate question unless it is somehow suggested that this witness was synchronising his reports. Now, is there anything else you want to ask about this judge's report? We may have to make it an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From what you say, that is that you asked the investigating judge to enter without a police escort, you said that the villagers were angry then that they were armed and that as soon as they saw the police, they would open fire. Is it true that the investigating judge asked you how come the villagers were armed? And instead of an answer, you threatened her and said that she would be to blame if there was fresh bloodshed and that he personally would then bring the judge in question before The Hague Tribunal. Was that your conversation with the lady, this investigating judge?

utterances.speaker: KAROL DREWIENKIEWICZ [Resumed]
